title: Should I buy a RM1 million landed house for my parents to live in?
excerpt: A Malaysian working in Singapore wants to buy her renting parents a landed home in Cheras. Sean explains why landed rents are so low, how to judge a renovated house, and a cheaper option first.

question.asker: From Miss R, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss R is in her mid-30s and works in Singapore. Her parents rent a house in the Cheras area and didn't like the condos they viewed, so she raised her budget for a landed house from RM800,000 to about RM1 million. Renovated houses ask around RM1 million while unrenovated ones nearby sell for RM800,000 to RM900,000, and similar houses rent for only about RM2,000 a month, less than half her expected instalment.
question.text: Is such a low rent normal for landed homes, and should she pay a premium for a renovated house, renovate an old one herself, or keep looking?

answer.quote: I don't think that renting is all that bad.
answer.summary: Yes, it is normal: a RM1 million landed house on a 90% loan costs about RM4,000 a month, while it rents for about RM2,000. Sean would first try to secure her parents' current rental with the landlord. If she still buys, choose between renovated and unrenovated by the bank's valuation and the cash she has left for works.

reasons.title: Landed homes rarely pay for themselves
reasons.body: Rent on a landed house is often barely half the instalment, which is why Sean favours high-rise units whose rent covers the loan. His one exception is a house near Johor's Second Link, where rent from cross-border workers almost covers the instalment.

reasons.title: Renting's only real risk can be managed
reasons.body: The setback of renting is the owner selling and asking the tenants to leave, so older people lose their neighbours and routines. A longer lease, and a written promise that the landlord offers them the house first if he sells, deals with most of that.

reasons.title: Banks value the house, not your renovation
reasons.body: A renovated house is worth the premium only if the bank values it near the asking price, so the loan covers it. Valuers count only legal structural extensions, usually for about three years. If a RM800,000 house values at RM850,000, the extra room helps pay for her own works.

reasons.title: Count the full cash before the keys
reasons.body: On a RM1 million house, about 18% up front for the down payment, stamp duty and legal fees, plus about RM200,000 of renovation, comes to roughly RM380,000. Renovating an old landed house from Singapore can also take three to six months.

actions: Ask her parents' landlord for a longer lease, a slightly lower rent, and first refusal in writing if the house is sold.
Use the money she saves to buy an investment unit whose rent covers its instalment.
If she buys, ask the agent for the bank's valuation of each house before deciding.
Budget the renovation separately from the loan she qualifies for.
Decide what will happen to the house later, including whether she may want to settle in Singapore.
caveat: Landed houses are one of a kind, so if her parents fall in love with one house and she has the capital, paying for it can still make sense. Sean also notes that many older people don't want to move, which argues for keeping them where they are.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #207. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in March 2023. Sean mentions he owns a landed house near Johor's Second Link whose rent almost covers its instalment.
